title: How full-stack works
canDo: explain how frontend, API and database fit together

blocks.md: You have React components that look great — but where does the data come from? Right now everything lives inside your JavaScript. The moment you refresh the page, it's gone. Real apps need a place to *store* data permanently and a way for the browser to talk to that store. That's full-stack: the browser (frontend) + a server (API) + a database — three layers that each do one job. This session maps out how those layers connect, then hands you the fastest on-ramp to building all three yourself.

By the end of this session you will be able to **explain how frontend, API and database fit together** — well enough to sketch the data flow on a whiteboard and choose the right layer for a piece of code.
blocks.canDo: explain how frontend, API and database fit together

blocks.md:
**Three layers, three jobs.**

- **Frontend** — React running in the browser. Shows UI, captures clicks. Has *no permanent memory*: every refresh starts fresh.
- **API** — code running on a server (Node, Python, etc.). Acts as a gatekeeper: it receives requests from the browser, enforces rules ("is this user logged in?"), then reads or writes data.
- **Database** — where data lives *permanently*. It never forgets. A relational database (like Postgres) stores data in tables you can query with SQL.

The browser *never* talks directly to the database — that would expose your data to anyone. It always goes through the API.

**Supabase** packages a Postgres database + an auto-generated REST/realtime API + built-in auth behind a single hosted service, so one developer can wire up all three layers in an afternoon.

blocks.md: **Mental model check:** when you click "Save" in a React form, the journey is: *React component → fetch/axios call → API route → database INSERT → response back up the chain → React re-renders with new data*. Each arrow is a network request or a SQL query. Supabase auto-generates the middle two steps for you.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a database in a full-stack app?
options: To render HTML to the user
To store data permanently so it survives page refreshes and server restarts
To validate form inputs before the user submits them
questions.explanation: A database stores data persistently — unlike in-memory JavaScript state, it survives refreshes, deploys, and restarts.

questions.question: In a typical full-stack architecture, which layer does the browser communicate with directly?
options: The database, via a direct SQL connection
The API (backend server), which then talks to the database
A CDN that caches all database rows
questions.explanation: The browser always talks to the API, never directly to the database — keeping credentials and business rules safely on the server.

questions.question: What does Supabase provide out of the box for a solo developer?
options: A React component library and CSS framework
A Postgres database, auto-generated API, and built-in auth — all hosted
A Node.js runtime you must configure and deploy yourself
A Git repository with CI/CD pipelines
questions.explanation: Supabase bundles Postgres + a REST/realtime API + auth into one hosted platform, letting one person build all three layers quickly.

blocks.md:
You can now describe the three-layer full-stack model: the **frontend** (React in the browser) sends requests to an **API** (server-side code), which reads and writes a **database** (permanent storage). Supabase collapses the API and database into a single managed service, making full-stack solo-developer projects practical.
